o: A server-side database table that stores user HTML
A place in client-side JavaScript where externally sourced data is processed in a way that can change what the browser parses or executes
A browser extension that blocks malicious scripts
A CSS property that hides dangerous elements from the DOM
questions.x: A sink is where data flows into something dangerous. Common examples include innerHTML assignments, eval calls, and location changes. If attacker-controlled data reaches a sink without sanitization, it can alter the DOM or run code.
questions.h: Sink means data flows into something. What kinds of JavaScript operations can turn user input into executable HTML or code?

questions.q: What is the relationship between a DOM source and a DOM sink in a DOM XSS bug?
o: Sources and sinks are the same thing in DOM XSS
A source is where attacker data enters the page, and a sink is where that data is processed dangerously, the bug exists when they are connected
Sources are always server-side and sinks are always client-side
A sink must come before a source in the JavaScript execution order
questions.x: DOM XSS requires data to flow from a source (URL parameter, postMessage, stored JSON) into a sink (innerHTML, eval). Neither alone is enough. The vulnerability is the path between them.
questions.h: Think of water flowing from a tap into a drain. Which is the source and which is the sink?

questions.q: Why is innerHTML considered a classic DOM sink?
o: innerHTML automatically executes all script tags in the string
The browser parses the assigned string as HTML, so tags and attributes in the data can create real elements and event handlers in the DOM
innerHTML sends the string to the server for validation before display
innerHTML only works with trusted same-origin content
questions.x:
Assigning a string to innerHTML runs the HTML parser on it. A payload like

can break out of the intended markup structure and inject executable attributes.
questions.h: innerHTML does not treat its input as plain text. What does the browser do with angle brackets in the string?

questions.q: Which of these DOM write operations is NOT a dangerous sink for HTML injection?
o: element.innerHTML = userInput
element.textContent = userInput
element.outerHTML = userInput
element.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', userInput)
questions.x: textContent and innerText treat input as plain text. The browser does not parse HTML tags from the string, so script tags and event handlers appear as literal text on screen rather than executing.
questions.h: One of these properties assigns text without running the HTML parser on the value.

questions.q: What is the difference between reflected DOM XSS and ordinary reflected XSS?
o: Reflected DOM XSS requires stored data, ordinary reflected XSS does not
In reflected DOM XSS the payload is read by client-side JavaScript from a source like a URL parameter and written to a sink, the server never echoes the payload in the HTML response
Reflected DOM XSS only works in Firefox
Ordinary reflected XSS uses innerHTML while DOM XSS uses eval exclusively
questions.x: Ordinary reflected XSS has the server embed the payload in the HTML response. Reflected DOM XSS has the server send clean HTML while client-side JavaScript reads the payload from the URL and passes it to a sink like innerHTML.
questions.h: In one case the payload appears in the page source from the server. In DOM XSS, where does the payload get read and where does it get written?
